REQUIRED, NOT DEFAULTED. .smoke_suite.json uses version: int = 1, which means a file with no version validates as version 1. The profile must not copy that: the field is required with no default, so a pre-versioning profile fails to validate loudly rather than being silently read as the current schema. That is the whole point of adding it.

The loader compares the file's version against the version this build writes and, on a mismatch, exits with a message that names both versions and says to reprofile. It does not attempt migration: this is a 0.x library, a profile is a cache that one instrumented run rebuilds, and migration code for a regenerable artefact is cost without benefit.
acceptance_criteria: ProfilingDataFile carries a required, non-defaulted schema version, written on capture and checked on load. A profile written by an older schema is rejected with a message naming the expected and found versions and telling the user to reprofile -- distinct from the message for a corrupt or unreadable file, and demonstrated by a test for each. cli.py's existing 'recorded by an older version' text is either made true or removed. No migration path. The version bump is noted in CHANGELOG.md as a breaking change.
notes: Blocks so-n6b.1 because n6b.1's hard-error-on-missing-scope behaviour cannot report itself accurately without a version to point at. Without one, 'this profile predates the recorded scope field' and 'this file is corrupt' are the same Pydantic ValidationError.
close_reason: ProfilingDataFile now carries a required, non-defaulted schema_version field (PROFILE_SCHEMA_VERSION=1). load_profiling_data_file checks it before Pydantic validation runs and raises ProfileSchemaMismatchError, which cli.py reports with a distinct message naming both versions and telling the user to reprofile -- separate from the generic 'failed to parse' message used for genuine corruption. The old 'recorded by an older version' guess is removed from the generic message. Noted in CHANGELOG.md as a breaking change. Tests cover both error paths in tests/test_profiler_models.py and tests/test_cli.py.

title: Nothing enforces that ProfilingData.tests keys match their outcome's test_id
description:
ProfilingData.tests is a dict[str, ProfilingOutcome] and ProfilingOutcome carries its own test_id, so a test's identity is stored twice with nothing keeping the two in step (smoke_optimiser/profiler/models.py:105, and ProfilingDataModel at :216).

Consumers have already diverged on which copy they read:
- smoke_optimiser/optimiser/greedy.py:172 uses the DICT KEY
- smoke_optimiser/downwind/maps.py _tests_by_file uses OUTCOME.TEST_ID

If a profile ever carries a mismatched pair, greedy selection and the downwind file -> tests map would disagree about what a test is called, and the downwind map would emit ids the runner cannot pass to pytest -- silently, since neither path validates.

The profile is loaded from JSON, so per the project's own rule ('data loaded from a file must be validated ... it may have been edited in between writing and reading') this is exactly the kind of correspondence ProfilingDataModel should be asserting rather than assuming. Noticed while building the downwind maps for so-n6b.8.

Fix: a model_validator on ProfilingDataModel rejecting any key that differs from its outcome's test_id, plus a test for the rejected case. Consider whether test_id should then be dropped from the outcome, leaving the key as the single source of identity.

title: snapshot() silently drops every edge touching a module with no __file__, such as a namespace package
description:
ImportTracer.snapshot builds `files`, a module-name -> project-path mapping, by
reading `__file__` off every module in sys.modules:

    file_attr = getattr(module, "__file__", None)
    if not file_attr:
        continue

then keeps only edges whose BOTH endpoints are in `files`:

    if edge.importer in files and edge.imported in files and ...

A module with no `__file__` is therefore dropped from the graph entirely, along with
every edge touching it, with no error and nothing counted. Namespace packages are
exactly this case: PEP 420 gives them `__file__ = None`, and any project laid out
without `__init__.py` files consists of them.

It currently fails SAFE rather than silently wrong -- the module is absent from
`files`, so it is absent from `unattributed_modules` too, so a change to it reads as
"no entry in the map" and runs the full suite. But that safety is incidental,
resting on a consumer rule that another issue could reasonably optimise away, and
the loss is invisible either way: a project could be missing a third of its graph
with every number in the profile looking healthy.

NEEDS A DECISION on the fix. A namespace package has no file to attribute an edge
to, but it does have `__path__`, and its submodules have real files; whether the
right answer is to resolve the package to its directory, to drop the edge but count
it beside resolution_errors, or to report the module as unattributed, is not
obvious. Whatever is chosen, the drop must stop being silent.
acceptance_criteria: A profile of a project using PEP 420 namespace packages either records edges for them or reports the loss in a countable field; in no case does the graph drop them while reporting zero errors. Covered by a test with a namespace-package fixture.

title: Record which importer each swallowed edge failure belonged to, so the doubt can be localised
description:
ImportTracer swallows edge-resolution failures into a bare count, because raising
inside __import__ would kill the suite being profiled. A count alone cannot be acted
on: it says some edges are missing without saying which, so a consumer can only
trust the whole graph or refuse the whole graph. Refusing it durably disables
change-based selection as the penalty for a defect that is OURS -- the failures are
our name arithmetic meeting legal Python, deterministic, and persisting until we fix
the tracer.

The failure loses the IMPORTED name, but the IMPORTER is still in hand at the point
of failure: _traced_import reads it from globals["__name__"], and
_traced_import_module from the caller frame it already walks. Recording it localises
the doubt, so selection can add the tests reaching those few modules and stay fast
everywhere else (the rule lives in so-n6b.2).

  - ImportGraph grows failed_importers, the modules whose edge recording failed,
    resolved to project-relative files at snapshot time like every other name.
  - Failures that occur BEFORE the importer can be read -- a globals mapping whose
    .get throws, or sys._getframe(1) raising -- have nothing to localise to. These
    are counted separately as unlocalised failures, and they are what still forces a
    full suite.
  - resolution_errors and error_samples stay as they are, for diagnosis.
  - Under xdist the sets union and the counts sum, like the rest of the graph.

Capturing the importer means reading it BEFORE the arithmetic that fails, so the
recording order in both wrappers changes: resolve the importer into a local, then
compute targets inside the try.
acceptance_criteria: A module whose edge arithmetic raises appears in ImportGraph.failed_importers as a project-relative path, while other modules' edges are unaffected. A failure occurring before the importer name is readable increments the unlocalised counter and adds nothing to failed_importers. Both merge correctly across xdist workers: sets union, counts sum.

title: Use the read map so a changed data file selects its readers instead of the whole suite
description:
so-n6b.3 records which files each test reads. This consumes that map, which turns
the blunt rule "a changed non-Python path is a blind spot, so run everything" into a
measured answer.

The rule this replaces is deliberately blunt because it has to be: without a read
map, a changed fixtures/rates.yaml and a changed README.md are the same input --
absent from a Python-execution map -- and only the full suite is safe for both.

With the read map:
  - a changed data file the map records reads of selects exactly the tests that
    read it;
  - a changed data file no test read, on a healthy map, selects nothing for that
    file, because the tracer watched every open for the whole suite. This is the
    only place in the design where absence is allowed to mean "nothing depends on
    this", and it is licensed by measurement, not assumption;
  - a changed file in the read map's unattributed set is a blind spot -> full suite;
  - environment-defining paths (uv.lock, pyproject.toml, Dockerfiles) remain a
    fixed full-suite rule, since nothing opens them during a run yet they change
    behaviour everywhere.

The read map may only ever ADD selections for Python files, never justify skipping
one. A C library calling fopen() raises no audit event, so a missing read edge is
undetectable, and the coverage and import relations remain the authority wherever
they have an opinion.
acceptance_criteria: A changed fixture that tests read selects exactly those tests. A changed file no test read, on a map with no unattributed reads, selects nothing and states that it was measured as unread. A changed file in the read map's unattributed set runs the full suite. A changed uv.lock, pyproject.toml or Dockerfile runs the full suite regardless of the read map.

title: Capture which files each test reads, so a changed data file is answerable instead of unknown
description:
Change-based selection can answer for a Python file two ways: coverage saw a test
execute it, or the import graph says a test's module depends on it. For a data file
-- a YAML or JSON fixture, a Jinja template, a golden/snapshot file, a .sql
migration -- it has neither relation, so absence from the map carries no
information at all. It means "we never looked", not "nothing reads this", and the
only safe reading of it is a full-suite run.

That is a real cost on real edits: today a README change and a fixture change are
indistinguishable, so both run everything.

This issue makes the relation measurable. Recording which file each test OPENS turns
absence into an answered negative: if the tracer watched every open for the whole
suite and nothing read README.md, then selecting no tests for a README edit is
justified by measurement rather than asserted by a config list. And when a docs test
does glob README.md, the tracer sees it and selects that test -- which an ignore
list would have got silently wrong.

MECHANISM: sys.addaudithook, one hook for the PEP 578 "open" event. Verified to
catch all three read paths uniformly, with the mode included so reads separate from
writes:

    open ('pyproject.toml', 'r', ...)      <- pathlib.Path.read_text
    open ('pyproject.toml', 'r', ...)      <- builtins.open
    open ('pyproject.toml', None, ...)     <- os.open, which bypasses both wrappers

One hook where the import tracer needed three patched mechanisms. Attribution is
also easier than for imports: the profiling hook already knows the active test node
id, so this is a direct file -> tests relation with no closure step.

SCOPE: reads only, project files only. Writes create no dependency. Paths outside
the repo root, and .venv/site-packages, tmp dirs, .pytest_cache and the coverage
database itself, are excluded.

BLIND SPOTS, which must be recorded rather than assumed away:
  - A file opened outside any test context (import time, collection) is recorded as
    UNATTRIBUTED, exactly as ImportGraph.unattributed_modules is. A change to one
    means the map cannot answer -> full suite. Reading it as "no test reads this"
    would be silent under-selection.
  - A C library calling fopen() directly raises no audit event. That is a missing
    edge with nothing to detect it, and it is the reason this map may only ever
    ADD selections, never justify skipping a Python file.
  - A conditionally-read file (warm vs cold cache) makes the map run-dependent in a
    way the import graph is not.

Environment-defining files stay a fixed full-suite rule regardless of this map:
uv.lock, pyproject.toml and Dockerfiles change behaviour everywhere while nothing
opens them during the run.

Scope here is CAPTURE ONLY. Consuming the map for selection is so-n6b.4.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - A user-configurable ignore list of test-irrelevant paths. Asserting what can be
    measured; wrong entries under-select silently, and it is a config surface we
    would then want to remove.
  - Wrapping builtins.open and io.open the way the import tracer wraps __import__.
    Misses os.open and anything holding an earlier reference; the audit hook is one
    mechanism that catches all of them.
acceptance_criteria: A profile records that a test reading fixtures/x.yaml via open(), Path.read_text() and os.open() depends on that file, in all three cases. A file read only at collection time is recorded as unattributed, not as unread. Writes create no entry. Files under .venv, tmp dirs and the coverage database are excluded. Verified serial and under xdist, where per-worker maps merge by union.

title: Localise import-graph failures: always run the tests reaching a module with a failed edge
description:
The import tracer swallows edge-resolution failures and counts them, because raising
inside __import__ would kill the suite being profiled. Every swallowed failure is a
MISSING EDGE, and a missing edge under-selects silently: if the lost edge was
tests/test_billing.py -> billing/rates.py, then editing rates.py does not select
test_billing, the commit goes green, and test_billing was the test that would have
caught the bug.

WHOSE DEFECT IT IS decides the policy. It is ours: the swallowed block does name
arithmetic only, so a failure is resolve_absolute_name or edge_targets meeting legal
Python it mishandles -- an unusual __package__, a namespace package, a module whose
globals lack __name__, an odd fromlist from a third-party caller of __import__. The
project cannot repair it; the error samples are a bug report addressed to us. The
user must not be made to pay a full suite on every commit for that, especially since
the failures are deterministic and will persist until we ship a fix.

LOCALISE THE DOUBT. The failure loses the IMPORTED name while the IMPORTER is still
in hand (so-n6b.5 records it). So the question "does changed file F affect module M"
is unanswerable for those M, and the sound rule is the inverse of a per-file
fallback: selection ALWAYS additionally runs every test whose closure reaches a
module in failed_importers. If three modules had failures, every selection carries
those three modules' dependents, every run, until the tracer is fixed. Bounded,
small, and safe by construction.

UNLOCALISED FAILURES -- where even the importer could not be read -- have nothing to
attach to and do force the full suite. Rare, and counted separately for exactly this
reason.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - Full suite on any non-zero resolution_errors, matching the time-based
    optimiser's refusal of an xdist profile. Consistent, but it disables the
    feature durably as the penalty for our own bug, and the xdist precedent differs:
    a parallel profile is something the USER chose and can undo.
  - A threshold on the error fraction. The number would be invented, and a single
    missing edge is enough to miss the one test that mattered.
  - Trusting the graph with a warning. That is the silent under-selection this line
    of work exists to prevent, with a warning attached.
  - Treating a change to a failed importer as unanswerable. Wrong direction: the
    lost half is what it imported, so a change to the importer itself is exactly the
    case we can still answer.
acceptance_criteria: Given a graph with failed_importers, every selection includes the tests whose closure reaches those modules, in addition to whatever the changed files select. A graph with unlocalised failures takes the full-suite path and names them as the reason. A graph with neither behaves exactly as it does today. The extra selection is reported, so a persistently degraded graph is visible rather than merely slow.
notes: Narrows the blunt rule so-jr5.2 ships with, where any non-zero resolution_errors makes the whole graph untrustworthy and forces the full suite. That is the safe direction, so this is a refinement: it converts a whole-graph refusal into the localised always-run set described above.

title: Expire a profile once a file exists that its downwind maps have never seen
description:
A profile can answer confidently and wrongly. Its downwind maps are a fact about the
codebase as it stood when it was captured, and nothing about a per-file lookup
notices that the codebase has moved on.

Concretely: the profile is captured at commit A. Since then a teammate added
billing/discounts.py and tests/test_discounts.py, and edited billing/rates.py so it
now imports discounts. You edit billing/rates.py. The maps HAVE an entry for it and
answer with the tests that touched it at commit A -- and test_discounts, which now
exercises rates through discounts, is not among them. Nothing tripped the
per-change fallback, because every file you touched was known. Silent
under-selection.

EXPIRY IS DIVERGENCE, NOT AGE. A profile is expired once a file exists that its maps
have never seen. That is the observable signature of the codebase having grown past
the map, and it is a fact rather than a threshold: no configured number, no
per-project tuning, nothing to get wrong. Compare the set of files that exist now
against ProfilingData.measured_files and the import graph's files.

Expired behaves exactly like absent: run the full suite. Because that fallback runs
instrumented and rewrites the profile, crossing the cliff costs one instrumented full
run rather than a full run on every commit until someone regenerates by hand.

so-n6b.7 measures how often the cliff is actually crossed. If it turns out to be
daily, this decision gets revisited against a real distribution.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - Wall-clock age past a configured threshold. A heuristic that reads a day of
    heavy refactoring as fresh and an untouched fortnight as stale, while measuring
    nothing that actually breaks the map.
  - A divergence threshold ("expired after N new files"). The number would be
    invented, and one new test file is enough to miss the test that mattered.
  - Selecting every collected test the profile has never seen, instead of expiring.
    Cheaper, and it does catch new test files -- but it leaves exactly the
    rates.py case above under-selecting, since the stale answer there involves no
    new test at all.
acceptance_criteria:
A profile is reported expired when a file IN SCOPE exists that is absent from both measured_files and the import graph -- equivalently, that DownwindMaps.knows() answers false for. IN SCOPE is defined by so-n6b.14: a .py file under the scope roots recorded in the profile at capture time, enumerated by plain 'git ls-files' (tracked files only).

A profile regenerated against an unchanged tree is NOT expired, demonstrated by a test that profiles, regenerates and asserts not-expired.

A non-Python file does not on its own expire a profile, and neither does a Python file outside the recorded scope. Both demonstrated; this repository's scripts/branch_summary.py is the live example of the second, tracked Python that no regeneration would ever teach the maps about.

A profile with no recorded scope is a HARD ERROR naming the fix (reprofile), not a silent full-suite run, carrying the schema version so-n6b.16 records so the message can say what is actually wrong.

It is not expired merely because time has passed, nor because existing files were edited. An expired profile takes the full-suite path with expiry named as the reason.
notes:
SCOPE comes from so-n6b.14: the coverage targets union the pytest test paths, resolved at capture time and recorded in the profile, so 'known to the maps' and 'in scope for expiry' cannot drift apart. A file in scope is one a freshly regenerated profile would know.

EXPIRY'S DOMAIN is tracked files you did NOT change -- the pull-or-checkout case, which is the only one no other rule sees. Files you did change, tracked or not, are so-7hr's changed set and are answered by so-jr5.2's unknown-changed-path rule. The two domains are disjoint by construction, so a given file has one reason rather than two.

The expiry TEST lives in so-jr5.2 as 'any(not maps.knows(p) for p in existing_files)', on the third input so-n6b.11 settled. so-jr5.4 enumerates and scopes existing_files; the rules stay pure and IO-free.

This issue expires on a changed TREE within a fixed scope. Expiring because the SCOPE itself changed is so-n6b.18: sound in principle, but it needs the effective scope of the next run to be knowable ahead of that run, which smoke-optimiser cannot currently determine.

title: Give the downwind selection its own file schema and pytest flag
description:
The downwind selection is written to a file that the pytest plugin reads, so pytest
runs the chosen node ids without a command line carrying a full suite's worth of
arguments.

IT IS ITS OWN FILE, WITH ITS OWN SCHEMA AND ITS OWN FLAG: `.downwind.json`, read
under `pytest --downwind`, with `--downwind-file-path` to relocate it. It shares
nothing with
SmokeSuiteFile but the list of node ids. SmokeSuiteFile exists to describe a
coverage bet: SummaryModel requires total_branches, full_suite_branches_covered,
smoke_branches_covered, smoke_coverage_pct and both runtimes; SmokeConfigModel
requires time_cap and target_cov; SelectedTestModel carries duration_s,
branches_covered, marginal_branches and efficiency. A downwind selection has no
time cap, no coverage target and no efficiency ranking, so every one of those fields
would be a zero, and the plugin's report header would announce "0.0% coverage" for a
selection making no coverage claim at all.

THE SCHEMA describes the categorical promise instead: the changed files it was
computed from, the node ids selected, the profile it was computed against, and --
when the answer is the full suite -- which blind spot forced it and why.
The reason is part of the file, not just console output, because it is what the
developer needs when the tool declines to select.

THE PLUGIN gets `--downwind` rather than teaching `--smoke` two meanings. Its report
header and its "test not found in collection" warning both currently assume the
coverage-suite framing and need their own wording here: a selected test missing from
collection means something different when the claim is categorical.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - One file with a mode discriminator and optional summary blocks. One flag for the
    user, but the schema then describes two unrelated things, every coverage field
    becomes optional, and the plugin branches on mode everywhere anyway.
  - Printing node ids for the caller to pass to pytest, with no file at all. Puts a
    full suite's worth of argv on the command line at 2600 tests, and the full-suite
    fallback must run through our own entry point for the instrumented rewrite to
    happen, so the caller cannot own the pytest invocation.
acceptance_criteria: A written selection file validates against its own model and carries the changed files, the selected node ids, the profile identity, and a reason when the answer is the full suite. The plugin run under its own flag collects exactly the listed node ids. The plugin's report header makes no coverage claim. .smoke_suite.json and the coverage-per-second path are untouched.

title: Collect the changed-file set from git: staged, unstaged and untracked, with renames and deletions
description:
Downwind selection needs the set of files that have changed, expressed the same way
the profile expresses paths.

THE CHANGED SET is the union of staged, unstaged and untracked changes. pytest reads
the WORKTREE, not the index, so a selection made from the index alone would run
tests against code the index does not contain -- testing something other than what
was measured. Untracked files are included: a brand new module has no map entry, so
it lands in the full-suite fallback, which is the right answer and only reachable if
the file is seen at all.

RENAMES are detected with -M and resolved to the OLD path. That is the only path the
profile knows, and a pure move is the common case; the alternative makes every
rename cost a full suite for nothing.

DELETIONS are looked up in the map exactly like any other change. The tests that
executed a deleted file are precisely the ones most likely to break, so nothing in
this path may gate on whether a path still exists on disk.

PATHS are repo-relative (so-746 makes the profile's paths repo-relative too), so the
two sides agree by construction.

Returns a typed result, not a bare list of strings: each entry carries its path and
its change kind, since the downwind rules treat a deletion, a rename and an addition
differently.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - Staged-only (git diff --cached), the obvious precommit choice. Rejected because
    pytest runs against the worktree.
  - Forgoing -M so a rename arrives as an add plus a delete. Correct but wasteful:
    the add is unknown, which forces a full suite on every move.
  - Taking the file list as an argument and doing no git work here. Rejected: the
    tool owns the promise, so it must own the definition of what it is promising
    about.
acceptance_criteria: A file edited but not staged appears in the set. An untracked file appears. A renamed file appears once, as its OLD path. A deleted file appears and is never filtered out for not existing. Every path is repo-relative regardless of the directory the command ran from. Each entry carries its change kind.

title: Make the profile's paths repo-relative, so git and the downwind maps agree by construction
description:
git reports paths relative to the REPOSITORY ROOT, whatever directory the command
ran from. The profile stores paths relative to PROJECT_ROOT, which cli.py sets to
Path.cwd(). These coincide only when smoke-optimiser happens to be run from the
repository root, and differ permanently in a monorepo where the Python project is
one directory of a larger repo -- exactly the layout where selecting a subset
matters most.

The failure mode is silence. A changed path 'services/api/db/models.py' is simply
absent from a map keyed by 'db/models.py', so it matches nothing and the selection
returns no tests for a file plenty of tests depend on.

THE REPOSITORY ROOT WINS, everywhere. `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` becomes the
root the profile's paths are relative to, so git and the map agree by construction
rather than by coincidence of the invocation directory. Outside a git repository the
root falls back to cwd, which is sound because downwind selection is
unavailable there anyway -- there is no diff to select from -- while profiling and
the coverage-per-second mode keep working.

THE PROFILE RECORDS ITS ROOT, as an absolute path. Without it a profile captured
under the old convention, or from a different checkout, matches nothing and reports
a healthy-looking zero; with it the mismatch is detectable and errors instead.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/cli.py (project_root), smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py
(relative_to), smoke_optimiser/profiler/import_tracer.py (snapshot's relative_to),
and the profile schema.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
  - Keeping cwd-relative paths and translating git's output at the point of use.
    Smaller change, but every future consumer of git output has to remember the
    translation, and forgetting it under-selects silently rather than failing.
  - Relying on the full-suite fallback to cover the mismatch. It does fail safe
    today, since every changed file looks new -- but only until something optimises
    that fallback away, and a systematic mismatch that looks like healthy operation
    is exactly what this design refuses to rely on.
acceptance_criteria: A profile captured from a subdirectory of a repository stores the same paths as one captured from the repository root. A changed file reported by git matches its map entry in a monorepo layout. A profile recorded against a different root is detected and errors rather than matching nothing. Outside a git repository, profiling still works with cwd as the root.
notes: Replaces the guard so-jr5.4 ships with, where downwind selection refuses to run unless invoked from the repository root, so cwd and the repository root provably coincide. The guard is sound but blocks the monorepo layout this feature is most valuable in, which is the whole point of doing this properly.

title: A missing import graph file is indistinguishable from a graph with no edges
description:
_read_iteration_graph (smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py) globs the temp directory for graph files, reads what it finds, and merges them:

    paths = sorted(import_graph_json.parent.glob(...))
    graphs = [read_graph(path) for path in paths]
    return merge_graphs(graphs)

With NO files present that is merge_graphs([]), which returns a perfectly valid
ImportGraph with no edges, no unattributed modules and no errors. Nothing raises.

WHY THAT IS DANGEROUS. An empty graph does not read as 'unknown', it reads as
'nothing in this project imports anything'. Every file then looks like a file no
module depends on, so change-based selection (so-jr5.2) would select no tests for a
change to any of them -- the silent under-selection this whole line of work
exists to prevent. Contrast the sibling path: _read_iteration_outcomes raises
OutcomesIngestError on an unreadable file, and a malformed graph raises
ImportGraphIngestError. Only ABSENCE is silent.

WHEN IT HAPPENS. pytest_unconfigure writes the graph, and it does not run if the
process is hard-killed (timeout, OOM, SIGKILL) -- see so-fp4 for the same class
of problem in the coverage database. Under xdist it is worse and more likely: one
killed worker means one missing file, so the merged graph silently lacks that
worker's edges while looking complete.

NEEDS A DESIGN DECISION. The runner knows how many graph files it should expect
in the serial case (exactly one), but under xdist it only learns the worker count
from the outcomes files it reads in the same iteration. Options: require at least
one graph file per iteration and error otherwise; cross-check the graph file count
against the worker count the outcomes reported; or have the hook write a sentinel
early so absence is detectable. Whatever is chosen, absence must not be silent.

title: CLI boolean defaults silently clobber the same setting from pyproject.toml
description:
resolve_config (smoke_optimiser/config.py) applies a CLI override whenever the value 'is not None'. Typer boolean flags default to False, not None, so they are ALWAYS applied.

Concretely: a project with

  [tool.smoke_optimiser]
  allow_ordered = true

still gets allow_ordered=False on every run that does not pass --allow-ordered, because the CLI's default False overrides it. The setting is silently inert -- the user sees the pytest-randomly error they configured away.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/cli.py builds cli_overrides with 'allow_ordered': allow_ordered; smoke_optimiser/config.py resolve_config's 'value is not None' loop.

The new --allow-parallel-durations flag (so-u3i) deliberately avoids this by passing 'allow_parallel_durations or None', which is the shape every boolean flag should use -- or resolve_config should learn which keys are booleans whose False means 'unset'. Pick one and apply it consistently.

NOT a theory: verified by reading the resolution loop, and the reason the new flag was written differently from its neighbour.

title: Fix lint errors after switching ruff to select=ALL
description: pyproject now selects ALL ruff rules; 55 errors across source, scripts and tests need fixing without editing lint rules.

title: A changed conftest.py puts every test at or below its directory downwind
description:
conftest.py is never imported by test modules -- pytest loads it itself -- so it has no edge in the import graph so-aeo captures, and its fixtures leave no distinguishing mark in files_covered either. Downwind selection would therefore see a changed conftest.py as affecting nothing, which UNDER-selects: silently skipping tests whose fixtures just changed is the worst failure this tool can have.

pytest's own rule is directory scope: a conftest.py applies to every test collected at or below the directory containing it. Mirror exactly that rule.
design:
Pure path-prefix matching against the collected test node ids, which already begin with a project-relative file path. For a changed file whose name is exactly 'conftest.py', select every test whose node id path is equal to or below that conftest's directory. A repository-root conftest.py therefore selects the whole suite, which is correct.

DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE -- these are separate, harder problems and must NOT be attempted here:
  - pytest_plugins declarations, which can load a conftest from an unrelated directory and break the directory-scope assumption.
  - Plugins supplied via -p on the command line.
  - Fixture-level granularity (working out WHICH fixtures a test actually used).
If the implementation starts needing any of these, stop and re-scope the issue rather than guessing.

Do not attempt to resolve a conftest's own imports here either; a conftest that imports a changed helper module is covered by so-aeo's graph, since conftest.py is itself an importer.
acceptance_criteria: A changed tests/sub/conftest.py selects every test under tests/sub/ and no test outside it. A changed conftest.py at the project root selects the entire suite. A changed conftest.py selects those tests even though no test module imports it and it contributes nothing to files_covered.
notes: Narrows the blunt rule so-jr5.2 ships with, where any changed conftest.py is a blind spot and runs the full suite. That rule over-selects rather than under-selects, so this is a refinement of a sound answer, not a fix for a broken one.

title: Hard-killed tests (timeout/crash) still produce orphaned coverage contexts and a misleading 'stale database' error
description:
Related to so-pc5 but NOT fixed by it. so-pc5's fix records an outcome whenever pytest's own makereport hook fires for a failed setup/teardown phase. But if a test's process is killed outright mid-phase -- e.g. pytest-timeout sending SIGKILL/SIGTERM, an OOM kill, or a segfaulting C extension under test -- makereport never runs for that phase at all. coverage.py may still have flushed a context row for whatever ran before the kill, but PYTEST_HOOK_CODE.pytest_runtest_makereport gets no chance to record anything for that nodeid.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py PYTEST_HOOK_CODE; smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py::_verify_contexts.

EFFECT: _verify_contexts still raises CoverageIngestError for that test id, and the message is still wrong for this cause specifically -- 'This usually means the coverage database is stale, or was combined across different runs; remove it and profile again' does not describe a hard-killed test, and removing the DB and re-profiling will reproduce the same failure if the kill is deterministic (e.g. a real timeout).

NEEDS A DESIGN DECISION: is this in scope to fix at all (vs. documenting it as a known limitation), and if so, how would we detect 'test process was killed' from the coverage DB side (no report was ever received) versus a genuinely stale/combined DB? At minimum the error message should stop asserting a single specific cause it cannot verify.

title: Multi-iteration duration averaging blends setup-phase duration from a differently-outcomed iteration
description:
Introduced by the so-pc5 fix (runner.py PYTEST_HOOK_CODE now also records failed setup/teardown reports).

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py, the iterations loop around lines 169-178:
  for nodeid, data in raw_outcomes.items():
      all_durations[nodeid].append(data['duration'])
      final_outcomes[nodeid] = data['passed']   # last iteration wins
      final_markers[nodeid] = frozenset(data['markers'])
avg_durations is then sum(all_durations[nodeid]) / len(...) across ALL iterations, unconditionally.

PROBLEM. With config.iterations > 1 and a flaky test whose fixture sometimes errors in setup:
  iteration 1: fixture errors in setup after doing 2.0s of work -> recorded passed=False, duration=2.0 (the setup phase duration)
  iteration 2: fixture succeeds, call passes in 0.01s -> recorded passed=True, duration=0.01
final_outcomes lands on passed=True (last iteration), but avg_durations averages 2.0 and 0.01 together (~1.0s) -- a passing test now reports a duration wildly inflated by an unrelated failing iteration's setup-phase timing.

Before so-pc5, failed iterations were absent from raw_outcomes entirely (the hook only recorded 'call'), so this contamination could not happen -- durations from failing iterations simply were not collected. so-pc5 fixed a real crash but reopened this averaging correctness gap as a side effect.

NEEDS A DESIGN DECISION: should durations only be averaged across iterations whose outcome matches final_outcomes (i.e. only average the 'passed' iterations' durations when the test ultimately counts as passed)? Or bucket durations by outcome and report the one matching final_outcomes? Or something else? This wasn't decided as part of so-pc5 since it's a distinct pre-existing averaging mechanism the fix newly interacts with.

title: Profiling ignores the project's own coverage config, inflating total_branches
description:
runner.py writes its own minimal rcfile and passes it as --cov-config, which
REPLACES the project's coverage configuration rather than extending it:

    COVERAGERC_CONTENT = '''
    [run]
    branch = True
    '''

So the project's own settings are silently discarded during profiling. Most
consequential is [report] exclude_lines. This repository's own pyproject.toml
has:

    exclude_lines = ['pragma: no cover', 'if TYPE_CHECKING:',
                     'def __repr__', 'raise NotImplementedError']

None of these apply while profiling. Branches the project has explicitly
declared un-coverable are therefore counted in total_branches, inflating the
denominator and depressing every reported coverage percentage. [run] omit and
[run] source are dropped for the same reason.

PRE-EXISTING, NOT A so-mr0 REGRESSION -- the old JSON path passed the same
rcfile to 'coverage json', so behaviour is unchanged. It is more VISIBLE now:
so-mr0 computes the denominator in-process from FileReporter using this rcfile,
so the exclusions are absent from both numerator and denominator, and
coverage_db is where the effect now lands.

INTERACTION WITH --target-cov: an inflated denominator makes a given
--target-cov harder to reach than the user intends, and can make a threshold
they set from 'coverage report' output unreachable.

DESIGN DECISION. Merging user config is not free: an omit or source setting that
conflicts with --src, or a dynamic_context already set to something other than
'test', would break profiling. Options are to layer our [run] settings over the
discovered config, or to read only [report] exclusions, or to keep replacing but
warn when the project has settings we are discarding.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py COVERAGERC_CONTENT; consumed by
smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py::read_coverage_db via config_file.

ACCEPTANCE: a branch marked 'pragma: no cover' does not appear in
total_branches, and profiling still works for a project with no coverage
configuration at all.

title: pytest's exit code is ignored, so a collection error silently yields a partial smoke suite
description:
runner.py runs the suite with check=False and never inspects the return code:

    subprocess.run(pytest_cmd, cwd=project_root, check=False, env=env)

Exit code 1 (tests failed) is expected and correctly handled -- failing tests are
hard-excluded. But every other non-zero code is swallowed:

  2  interrupted (e.g. Ctrl-C, or --maxfail reached)
  3  internal error
  4  usage error (e.g. a bad --pytest-args value)
  5  no tests collected

A COLLECTION ERROR IN ONE FILE is the dangerous case. pytest still runs and
still writes coverage for everything it did collect, so profiling proceeds
happily and emits a smoke suite that is simply missing every test in the broken
file. The user gets a green-looking result that under-selects, with no
indication anything was skipped. That is precisely the silent under-selection
so-mr0 was written to eliminate -- so-mr0 closed the ingest hole but this one is
upstream of it and still open.

Exit 5 (no tests collected) is currently caught downstream by chance: no
coverage database means CoverageIngestError. The message will talk about a
missing database rather than about no tests being collected.

DECISION NEEDED on --iterations > 1: if iteration 3 of 5 is interrupted, is the
accumulated coverage still usable, or is the whole run void? Coverage
accumulates across iterations into one database, so a partial iteration
contributes real data but skews nothing except durations.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py:157

ACCEPTANCE: a project with one uncollectable test file fails loudly rather than
producing a smoke suite; exit code 1 still proceeds as it does today.

title: Expire a profile when its recorded scope no longer covers what the next run would measure
description:
so-n6b.14 records the scope roots a profile was captured under, and so-n6b.1 expires a profile when an in-scope file is unknown to its maps. Neither notices when the SCOPE ITSELF changes. Widen --cov from smoke_optimiser to smoke_optimiser and scripts, and a whole tree becomes knowable that the maps have never seen: a regenerated profile would know it, the current one never will, and nothing expires. That is silent staleness of exactly the kind so-n6b.1 exists to prevent, arriving through configuration rather than through the tree.

THE HARD PART IS COMPUTING WHAT TO COMPARE AGAINST, and it is why this is not a one-line set comparison bolted onto so-n6b.1.

Deciding drift means knowing the scope the NEXT run would measure, ahead of running it. smoke-optimiser cannot currently determine that. runner.py:290-298 appends --cov={config.cov_source} only when config.pytest_args lacks a --cov, and nothing anywhere inspects the project's own [tool.pytest.ini_options] addopts -- pytest applies those itself, invisibly. This repository is the case in point: pyproject.toml:67 carries --cov=smoke_optimiser, and config.py's _discover_cov_target independently arrives at the same answer by a different route. On a project where those two disagree, a naive 'recorded != currently resolved' test is TRUE ON EVERY RUN AGAINST AN UNTOUCHED TREE -- the profile is born expired, every run takes the full-suite path, so-jr5.3 rewrites the profile, and the next run is expired again. That is precisely the failure so-n6b.14 was raised to eliminate, reintroduced through the comparison meant to strengthen it.

So this issue must first make the effective scope knowable ahead of a run -- by reading the project's pytest configuration the way pytest resolves it, or by probing (a collect-only run reporting the resolved --cov targets), or by another route that cannot disagree with what the profiling run will actually measure. Recording the scope is sound precisely because it observes the run; recomputing it must reach the same answer or it is worse than nothing.

SUBSET, NOT EQUALITY. Widening must expire: files become knowable that the maps have never seen. Narrowing must not: every file still in scope is one the maps already know, so the maps become a superset of what is asked of them, which is safe. Expiring on a narrowing costs one instrumented full run (so-jr5.3) for a configuration change that made the tool's job smaller. The test is 'the resolved scope is not a subset of the recorded scope', over normalised repo-relative roots by PREFIX -- smoke_optimiser/downwind is inside smoke_optimiser by prefix, not by string equality. Getting that backwards, and reading a widening as a narrowing, restores the silent staleness this issue exists to close.

COMPARE RESOLVED ROOTS, NEVER CONFIGURATION TEXT. Reordering flags, or adding an unrelated pytest option, must not expire a profile.

ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED, do not re-propose:
• Compare recorded roots against config.cov_source union testpaths directly. This is the naive test above; it is unsound wherever the project's addopts carry a --cov, which is common and is true of this repository.
• Hash the addopts string. Expires on whitespace, flag order and unrelated options, and does not expire when the same scope is reached by a different route.
• Skip drift detection and rely on the tree comparison. That is so-n6b.1's MVP position and is safe but incomplete: a widened scope never expires, so the newly-in-scope tree stays permanently invisible.
acceptance_criteria: Widening the profiling scope expires the profile. Narrowing it does not, and the resulting selection for an in-scope changed file is unchanged -- a test for each. A project whose pytest addopts carry a --cov that differs from what config.py's _discover_cov_target returns is NOT expired on an untouched tree; this is the regression test that the naive comparison fails. The subset test is on normalised repo-relative roots by prefix, with a test distinguishing a prefix match from a string match. Reordering pytest flags does not expire a profile.
notes:
The soundness constraint is the whole issue. A drift check that can be permanently true is strictly worse than no drift check, because it pins the tool to the full-suite path forever while looking like it is working -- and so-jr5.3's instrumented fallback makes the loop self-sustaining and silent.

Covers the widening/narrowing asymmetry as well as the detection itself, so the correct semantics land in one piece rather than as a strict rule followed by a relaxation.

title: Repair an expired profile by running only the new test files, not the whole suite
description:
so-n6b.1 makes 'expired behaves exactly like absent: run the full suite', and so-jr5.3 runs that fallback instrumented so it rewrites the profile. That is the right MVP answer, and it is correct in every case. It is not always the CHEAPEST correct answer.

SCOPED DELIBERATELY TO ONE CASE: the only in-scope files unknown to the maps are new TEST files. Nothing else about the divergence -- no new source file, no new package. Adding a new source file keeps the full-suite fallback; there is no principled cheap repair there, because the new module is reached from existing files whose test attribution may have changed in ways only rerunning those tests can reveal.

In the new-test-file-only case the missing information is exactly what running those files produces. Running tests/test_discounts.py under instrumentation yields its coverage contexts, so the file -> tests map gains test_discounts against every file it executed, including the existing files it reaches transitively. That is the entry the stale profile was missing in so-n6b.1's own worked example -- a teammate's new test that exercises rates.py through discounts.py, invisible to a profile captured before it existed.

The import graph half is cheaper still. The tracer installs at pytest_configure specifically because project modules are imported during collection (runner.py:66-68), so a --collect-only pass rebuilds the whole graph without executing a single test. merge_graphs already exists in import_tracer.py.

WHAT MAKES IT HARDER THAN IT LOOKS, and why it is not part of the MVP:

• The merged profile is assembled from one tree state for most tests and another for the new ones, so ProfilingMeta.commit names only one of them. What the metadata MEANS after a partial merge needs deciding, not inheriting.
• _verify_contexts asserts the coverage contexts match the tests that ran. A partial run covers a fraction of the suite, so the check must distinguish 'partial by design' from the incomplete-data case so-jr5.3 exists to catch. Getting that wrong reintroduces exactly the silent partial-profile overwrite jr5.3's 'MUST NOT OVERWRITE A GOOD PROFILE WITH A PARTIAL ONE' guards against.
• unattributed_modules does not union cleanly: a module attributed in the full run may be unattributable in a partial one, because its importer was never loaded. Union grows the unattributed set, which is conservative (more refusals) rather than unsafe, but it means repeated partial repairs degrade the graph over time. Needs a bound.

GATED ON so-n6b.7. If new files arrive weekly the cliff is free and this is unnecessary complexity on the most safety-critical path in the tool. If they arrive daily -- and n6b.7 is being widened to report new TEST files separately, which is precisely this issue's population -- the saving is most of a suite most days. Do not start this before that distribution exists.
acceptance_criteria: An expired profile whose only unknown in-scope files are test files is repaired by running just those files under instrumentation, and the resulting selection matches what a full instrumented re-profile would have selected -- demonstrated by a test that constructs both and compares. Any other cause of expiry still takes the full-suite path. The merged profile's metadata states what it is, and a partial run that fails to produce complete data leaves the previous profile in place, per so-jr5.3. Repeated partial repairs do not monotonically grow unattributed_modules.
notes:
Scoped deliberately to the new-test-file case. Adding a new source file keeps the full-suite fallback: the new module is reached from existing files whose test attribution may have changed in ways only rerunning those tests can reveal, so there is no principled cheap repair.

This changes the RESPONSE to expiry, not the test for it. so-n6b.1's definition of expiry is untouched; what it supersedes is n6b.1's 'expired behaves exactly like absent', in this one case.

ALTERNATIVE CONSIDERED: repair from a --collect-only pass alone. That rebuilds the whole import graph for almost nothing, since the tracer installs at pytest_configure precisely because project modules are imported during collection. But it yields no coverage contexts, so the file -> tests map gains nothing -- and the file -> tests map is the half a new test file actually changes. The collect-only pass is worth doing as part of this, not instead of it.

title: Expire on a scope change only when the new scope is not a subset of the recorded one
description:
so-n6b.14 settled that a profile expires when its recorded scope roots differ from the ones the current configuration resolves to. For the MVP that is 'any difference', chosen for being one comparison with nothing to get wrong.

Any difference is stricter than necessary in one direction. WIDENING the scope must expire: new files become knowable, and a regenerated profile would know them, so the maps are stale in exactly so-n6b.1's sense. NARROWING cannot cause under-selection. If the scope goes from --cov=smoke_optimiser to --cov=smoke_optimiser/downwind, every file still in scope is one the maps already know -- the maps become a superset of what is asked of them, which is safe. Expiring there buys nothing and costs one instrumented full run (so-jr5.3), for a configuration change that made the tool's job smaller.

The refinement: expire when the current scope is not a subset of the recorded scope, rather than when the two differ.

Subset over roots, not over paths -- 'smoke_optimiser/downwind' is a subset of 'smoke_optimiser' by prefix, not by string equality, so the comparison is on normalised, repo-relative root paths with a prefix test. Getting that wrong in the unsafe direction (treating a widening as a narrowing) reintroduces the silent staleness so-n6b.14 exists to close, which is why it is a refinement rather than the MVP behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: Widening the profiling scope still expires the profile. Narrowing it does not, and the resulting selection is still correct -- demonstrated by a test that narrows the scope, asserts not-expired, and asserts the selection for an in-scope changed file is unchanged. The subset test is on normalised repo-relative root paths by prefix, with a test for the case that distinguishes a prefix match from a string match.
notes: Not blocking so-n6b.1: the MVP behaviour is correct, merely conservative. A narrowed scope costs one instrumented full run (so-jr5.3) for a configuration change that made the tool's job smaller, which is wasteful rather than wrong.

title: _tests_by_file silently drops a covered file that known_files does not contain
description:
Noticed while reading smoke_optimiser/downwind/maps.py during so-n6b.10.

_tests_by_file (maps.py:69) inverts every outcome's files_covered into 'covering', then returns a dict comprehension over known_files ONLY:

    return {path: frozenset(covering.get(path, ())) for path in known_files}

Any path a test actually executed that is absent from known_files is discarded without trace. known_files (maps.py:57) is measured_files | the graph's edge endpoints | unattributed_modules, so this rests on the unstated invariant that files_covered is a subset of measured_files for every outcome.

That invariant is plausible but not enforced anywhere, and there is at least one live reason to doubt it: so-746 records that the profile's paths are not yet repo-relative by construction, so files_covered and measured_files can be normalised differently and fail to match as strings even when they name the same file.

The consequence is not a wrong answer -- a dropped path is absent from known_files, so knows() is False, so jr5.2 refuses and runs the full suite. It fails in the safe direction. But it is silent: real coverage evidence we HELD is thrown away, and the resulting full-suite run is indistinguishable from a genuinely unknown file. In a component whose entire purpose is to make 'the map cannot answer' explicit rather than implicit, discarding an answer we had is worth making visible.

Fix is either to fold covering's keys into known_files (so a covered file is known by construction), or to assert the invariant and let a violation be loud. Which one depends on whether a covered-but-unmeasured file is considered possible at all -- so-746 may make the question moot by fixing the normalisation upstream.
acceptance_criteria: A file appearing in some outcome's files_covered but not in measured_files or the import graph is either folded into known_files or raises, rather than being silently dropped. Covered by a unit test over a hand-built profile with exactly that mismatch.

title: so-n6b.1's timezone acceptance criterion is a leak from the wall-clock expiry it rejected
description:
Noticed while settling so-n6b.10, which was the same class of defect: an acceptance criterion that contradicts its own issue's description.

so-n6b.1's description is emphatic that expiry is divergence and NOT age -- 'EXPIRY IS DIVERGENCE, NOT AGE ... it is a fact rather than a threshold: no configured number, no per-project tuning' -- and its ALTERNATIVES CONSIDERED explicitly rejects 'Wall-clock age past a configured threshold', marked do-not-re-propose.

Its acceptance criteria nonetheless end with: 'Timezone-aware comparison wherever capture time is read.'

Under the divergence rule, capture time is never read. The test is a set comparison between the repository's current files and measured_files | the import graph's files; ProfilingMeta.timestamp plays no part. The criterion is a vestige of the rejected age-based design, and it is actively misleading: an implementer reading the acceptance criteria for a definition of done will look for a datetime comparison that should not exist, and may add one.

The project's timezone-awareness rule (GEMINI.md) is real and applies wherever datetimes ARE used -- ProfilingMeta.timestamp is one such place. But it is a global standing rule, not an acceptance criterion for this issue.

Fix: strike the sentence from so-n6b.1's acceptance criteria. No code change.
acceptance_criteria: so-n6b.1's acceptance criteria no longer reference capture time or timezone-aware comparison, and describe only the divergence test its description specifies.

title: DownwindMaps.dependents_of does a fresh per-file graph walk instead of SCC-based memoization
description:
smoke_optimiser/downwind/maps.py's _closure() deliberately walks the dependents graph fresh for every file (O(V*(V+E)) worst case across the whole map) rather than memoizing per node, because naive per-node memoization can cache an incomplete closure computed mid-cycle. This is documented in the function's docstring as a correctness-over-performance tradeoff.

At the repo scales measured so far (smoke-optimiser ~35 files/91 edges, casey_ai/api 143 files, enphase_curtailer 271 files) this is fast (sub-millisecond to build the whole map). It could become a real cost on a much larger monorepo (thousands of files). The correct fix if it ever matters is Tarjan/Kosaraju SCC condensation: compute strongly-connected components once, closure each component as a unit (which also gets cycle self-inclusion for free), then propagate over the condensation DAG in reverse topological order -- rather than a fresh walk per node.

Not worth doing speculatively; filed so the tradeoff and its fix are recorded rather than rediscovered. Only act on this if profile-build time on a real project is measured to actually be a problem.
acceptance_criteria: Either closed as won't-fix with a measurement showing build time is fine at real project scale, or DownwindMaps._dependents_by_file is rewritten using SCC condensation with the same public behaviour and existing tests still passing.

title: Measure how often a new file appears, since that is what expires a profile
description:
A profile is expired once a file exists that its map has never seen, which is a
cliff: crossing it costs one instrumented full run, which rewrites the profile and
resets it.

Nobody has measured how often that is. If a working week of ordinary development
adds a file most days, the cliff is crossed most days and downwind selection is
worth much less than the median-37-of-2600 headline suggests. If it is crossed
weekly, it is free.

MEASURE, over the last few months of history in smoke-optimiser, casey_ai and
enphase_curtailer: for each commit, how many commits (and how much wall-clock time)
pass before a file appears that did not exist at that commit. Report the
distribution, not a mean -- the interesting number is how often the interval is
short enough to matter.

The result decides whether the divergence cliff needs softening, and if so it gives
a real distribution to design against instead of an invented threshold. It also
prices the alternative that was rejected on principle: a wall-clock expiry is only
worse than divergence if divergence is actually cheaper to live with.
acceptance_criteria:
A reported distribution of the interval between a commit and the next commit introducing a file it did not have, in commits and in wall-clock time, across all three repositories.

BROKEN DOWN BY, because the aggregate interval alone cannot price the alternatives:
• New TEST files separately from new SOURCE files. so-n6b.17 can repair the test-file case by running only those files, so the two populations have different costs and only the source-file interval prices the true cliff.
• Files IN SCOPE separately from files outside it, on the scope so-n6b.14 settled (the coverage targets union the pytest test paths). A new file outside that scope never expires anything, so counting it inflates the cliff rate.
• Files git TRACKS separately from untracked ones. so-n6b.14 settled that expiry enumerates tracked files only, on the basis that an untracked file is one you just created and so-7hr already puts it in the changed set. If the untracked population turns out to be large, that reasoning is worth rechecking against it.
notes: The breakdowns are not incidental. The aggregate interval cannot distinguish the case so-n6b.17 can repair cheaply (new test files) from the one that stays expensive (new source files), and under so-n6b.14's scope some new files never expire a profile at all. Asking for the splits up front costs the measurement script almost nothing; retrofitting them means running the history again.

title: ProfilingData uses two words for one concept: unattributable_branches but unattributed_modules
description:
ProfilingData carries unattributable_branches (added by an earlier issue) and ImportGraph carries unattributed_modules (added by so-aeo). They name the same idea -- something the profile observed but could not tie to a test -- with two different words, in adjacent fields of the same dataclass tree.

The existing convention across the codebase is 'unattributable': coverage_db.py
uses it for the local variable, the frozen dataclass field and the comment
explaining the summarised context list. so-aeo introduced 'unattributed' without
noticing, so the new field is the odd one out and should be the one to change.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/models.py (ImportGraph field and docstring,
ImportGraphModel field), smoke_optimiser/profiler/import_tracer.py (snapshot,
merge_graphs, write_graph, module docstring), smoke_optimiser/cli.py
(_save_profiling_data), tests/test_import_tracer.py and
tests/test_profiler_models.py.

Note this is a profile format change: the field name appears in the JSON, so an
existing .smoke_profiling_data.json fails validation afterwards and must be
regenerated. That is the established behaviour for this file (see so-d8v and
so-aeo, which both made new fields required for the same reason), but it is worth
doing before so-jr5.2 starts reading the field rather than after.

Too small to be urgent, too easy to fix later to leave undecided.

title: Measure the import tracer's overhead on a large suite
description:
so-aeo added an ImportTracer that replaces builtins.__import__ and importlib.import_module for the whole profiling run. Every execution of every import statement in the suite now goes through a Python-level wrapper that resolves the target name, walks its ancestors and updates a set.

The cost is UNMEASURED. On smoke-optimiser itself the suite is far too small and
too fast for the difference to be distinguishable from noise, so nothing here
tells us what it does to a real suite.

This matters because so-jr5.3's whole argument for regenerating the profile in the
background rests on profiling being cheap: it quotes a measured +11% for coverage
instrumentation on enphase_curtailer (61s -> 68s with --cov-context=test). If the
tracer adds materially to that, the trade-off changes, and the capture may need to
become optional rather than always-on.

WHAT TO DO. Profile a large suite (enphase_curtailer, 2600 tests, or casey_ai/api,
1389 tests) three ways -- plain, with coverage instrumentation only, and with
instrumentation plus the tracer -- and record the deltas. The comparison needs the
tracer to be switchable to run at all, which is itself a useful outcome: today it
installs unconditionally from the profiling hook.

If the overhead is small, record the number next to the +11% in so-n6b and close
this. If it is not, file the follow-up to make capture optional.

title: The canonical repro command emitted --no-allow-ordered, which the CLI rejects
description:
build_repro_command emitted '--no-allow-ordered' when allow_ordered was off, but --allow-ordered is declared as a bare flag with no negative form. Pasting the 'Repro:' line printed in the summary therefore failed with 'No such option: --no-allow-ordered' -- the one command whose entire job is to reproduce the run did not run.

Verified before the fix:
  $ uv run smoke-optimiser --no-allow-ordered --optimise-only
  Error: No such option: --no-allow-ordered  Did you mean --allow-ordered?

FIXED while implementing so-u3i, since that issue added a second boolean flag and copying the broken shape was not an option. Boolean flags are now emitted only in their positive form and omitted when off. tests/test_reports.py asserts the absent case explicitly, and the completeness test now turns every boolean on so each must be named.

Filed after the fact so the history exists.
close_reason: Fixed as part of so-u3i; boolean flags now emit only their positive form and tests cover both the present and absent cases.

title: Ingest assumes every measured file is Python, so honouring a project's coverage plugins would crash on template files
description:
read_coverage_db in smoke_optimiser/profiler/coverage_db.py builds a PythonFileReporter for every row in the coverage database's file table:

    reporter = PythonFileReporter(absolute_path, cov)

coverage.py supports file-type plugins (django_coverage_plugin, mako, jinja) which put NON-Python files into that same table and supply their own FileReporter implementation. Asking PythonFileReporter to parse a .html template will fail, and the failure lands in a code path whose stated stance is that every error is fatal -- so profiling would abort outright on any project using one of these plugins.

LATENT TODAY, REACHABLE THE MOMENT so-asl LANDS. runner.py currently replaces the project's coverage configuration with a minimal rcfile containing only 'branch = True', which discards any configured plugins along with everything else. So the file table is Python-only by accident. so-asl exists precisely to stop discarding the project's config; the moment it does, plugin-registered files start appearing and this crashes. The two must land together.

The correct fix is to ask coverage for the right reporter rather than hard-coding one -- coverage's own reporting layer resolves a FileReporter per file via its plugin registry. Whether non-Python files should then contribute branches to the map at all is a design question worth deciding explicitly rather than falling out of the implementation: a template's 'branches' may not be a meaningful selection signal.
acceptance_criteria: A coverage database containing a file registered by a coverage file-type plugin is ingested without error, and the decision about whether such files contribute branches is documented rather than incidental.

title: Profile JSON is written in non-deterministic order, so two identical profiling runs produce byte-different files
description:
_save_profiling_data in smoke_optimiser/cli.py serialises every frozenset with bare list(), which takes Python's set iteration order:

    branches_covered=list(po.branches_covered)
    files_covered=list(po.files_covered)
    markers=list(po.markers)
    total_branches=list(profiling_data.total_branches)
    measured_files=list(profiling_data.measured_files)
    unattributable_branches=list(profiling_data.unattributable_branches)

Set ordering varies with insertion history and string hashing, so profiling the same tree twice yields JSON that differs everywhere despite describing identical data. That makes profiles impossible to diff, impossible to check into a repository usefully, and hides real changes in the noise -- which matters as soon as anyone wants to see what a code change did to the coverage map.

Sorting is the obvious fix. Note it is six lines, all in one function, which is why this is filed rather than fixed inline. Consider whether sorting belongs in the model layer instead, so anything else that serialises a profile inherits it.

Sizes are modest -- this repository has a few hundred branches, enphase_curtailer's 2600-test suite would be in the low tens of thousands -- so the sort cost is not a concern at realistic scale.
acceptance_criteria: Profiling the same tree twice with no source changes produces byte-identical JSON, ignoring the meta block's timestamp and command.

title: Parallel pytest workers (xdist) would race on the single shared outcomes JSON file
design:
DECIDED 2026-09-06 (user): SUPPORT xdist, do not reject it.

RATIONALE. Half this tool is the coverage map, half is the time-based suite
construction. Wanting only the map is a completely normal use (so-jr5's
change-based selection consumes the map and never reads a duration). Parallel
profiling is fine for that half, so it must not warn loudly at profile time.
Contended durations only matter to the half that uses time, so that is the
half that objects.

CAPTURE. Per-worker outcomes files keyed by PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER, merged by the
runner after the run (union across files). Detection must be RUNTIME, not
arg-string sniffing: xdist can be switched on by the target project's own
pytest.ini addopts, never appearing in --pytest-args, which is the exact
silent-data-loss case this issue is about. The plugin reads PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER
and PYTEST_XDIST_WORKER_COUNT from its own process.

RECORD. The worker count lands in the profile (ProfilingMeta), so the fact
travels with the artefact rather than living in stderr.

CONSUME. The time-based optimiser ERRORS on a profile recorded with >1 worker,
with an explicit override flag to proceed. A coverage-per-second ranking built
on contended timings is confidently wrong and looks fine, so a warning is not
enough. The map-only consumers stay silent.
close_reason: xdist supported: per-worker outcomes files merged by the runner, worker count recorded in the profile, time-based optimiser errors on a parallel profile with an --allow-parallel-durations override. Verified end to end with real pytest-xdist: 93/93 tests captured across 2 workers.

title: check_prerequisites looks for pytest on PATH but the runner invokes it as a module
description:
check_prerequisites gates on pytest being an executable on PATH:

    if shutil.which('pytest') is None:
        raise RuntimeError('pytest not found in PATH')

but every actual invocation runs it as a module of the current interpreter:

    pytest_cmd = [sys.executable, '-m', 'pytest', ...]

The two can disagree in both directions.

FALSE NEGATIVE (the common one): pytest is importable by sys.executable but not
on PATH. This is normal when smoke-optimiser is invoked via 'uv run', via
'python -m', from a virtualenv whose bin directory is not on PATH, or from a
tox/nox session. Profiling is refused even though it would work.

FALSE POSITIVE: a pytest on PATH belonging to a DIFFERENT environment satisfies
the check while sys.executable has no pytest, so the check passes and the
subprocess then fails with 'No module named pytest'.

FIX: test what is actually used -- importlib.util.find_spec('pytest') against
the running interpreter -- and say which interpreter was checked when it fails.

WHERE: smoke_optimiser/profiler/runner.py:58

NOTE: tests/test_runner.py::test_check_prerequisites_success patches
shutil.which, so the patch target moves with the fix.

ACCEPTANCE: profiling proceeds in an environment where pytest is importable but
absent from PATH.

title: Line-level downwind selection, with git-aware remapping of shifted line numbers
description:
so-n6b deliberately ships FILE-level downwind selection: a changed file
selects every test that has ever executed any line in it. This is the follow-up
that narrows it to the lines actually touched.

WHY IT WAS NOT DONE FIRST. Line numbers shift. Insert one line at the top of a
file and every line number below it moves, so a line-level map silently
mismatches after almost any edit -- and silent mismatch means silent
under-selection, the one failure mode this feature must never have. File-level
is immune to line shifts, reformatting, and refactors within a file.

WHAT THIS NEEDS. Git-aware remapping: track how lines moved between the commit
the profile was taken at (ProfilingMeta.commit is already recorded) and HEAD, so
a profiled line number still resolves to the right line today. `git diff -U0`
between those two commits gives the hunks to translate through.

DO NOT START THIS UNTIL file-level has been measured in real use. On enphase the
file-level map has a median of 37 tests per file out of 2600 -- if that is
already fast enough, the extra precision buys nothing and costs a whole
remapping layer that can be subtly wrong.
